summary: Defines an architecture for Open Pluggable Edge Services, in which a data provider, a data consumer and optional intermediary entities cooperate to apply services to a data stream. It describes the building blocks that let services be inserted at network edges.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a parcel moving down a conveyor belt where helpers along the way can add a label or check the contents. This document describes the belt and helpers.

questions: what is an opes data dispatcher
what is an opes trust domain
subtitle: How a data stream can be analyzed or transformed by cooperating services placed between provider and consumer.

tldr.problem: Some services on a data stream, such as customizing content for a consumer's display, are best or only deployable at a network location between provider and consumer.
tldr.mechanism: OPES defines entities (service applications and data dispatchers inside OPES processors), flows, and rules that say when to run services, with optional remote callout servers reached by the OPES callout protocol.
tldr.outcome: The architecture requires consent, IP-layer addressability, tracing and trust-aware security, and leaves few other interoperability requirements.

today: RFC 3835 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The callout protocol requirements it relies on are in RFC 3836.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A data stream service between a data provider and a data consumer may need extra application entities, for example to customize the stream based on the consumer's display capabilities. It can be useful to do this at a network location between the two, and for some services performed on behalf of the end user it may be the only option.

This document presents the architectural components of Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) needed for such a service. It addresses the IAB considerations in RFC 3238 and recommends reading the use cases document, RFC 3752, first.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a helper standing between you and the shop can tailor what you get, such as making a picture fit your screen.

sections.title: Entities, Flows and Rules
sections.content:
The architecture has three concepts. OPES entities are processes in the network; OPES flows are data flows realized by those entities; OPES rules specify when and how to run services.

An OPES entity is either an OPES service application, which analyzes and possibly transforms messages, or a data dispatcher, which invokes a service application based on a ruleset and application-specific knowledge. Entities live inside OPES processors, and a processor MUST include a data dispatcher. The provider and consumer applications are not OPES entities. HTTP is used as the example underlying protocol.

An OPES flow needs at least one data dispatcher, and may have many. A ruleset is made of conditions and related actions, and all dispatchers are invoked for all flows. The ruleset schema must be standardized, but how a ruleset is loaded into a dispatcher is a local matter.
sections.plainLanguage: The belt is the flow, the helpers are entities, and the rule book tells each helper when to step in.

sections.title: Callout Servers and Tracing
sections.content:
A processor may spread the work by contacting one or more callout servers. The data dispatcher does this with the OPES callout protocol (OCP), whose requirements are in RFC 3836. The OCP is application-agnostic, but the dispatcher MUST have a service-aware vectoring capability that parses the flow according to the ruleset and delivers data to the local or remote service application.

Every data dispatcher MUST provide tracing so its operation can be verified. Tracing must be feasible on the flow, per OPES processor, using in-band annotation. This MAY require header extensions in the application protocol, but an OPES processor SHALL NOT interfere with non-OPES clients and servers. Processors MUST obey tracing, reporting and notification requirements set by the center of authority in their trust domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper hands the job to a specialist, it uses an agreed way of passing it, and every helper must leave a note saying what it did.

sections.title: Trust, Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Each data flow MUST be secured according to several policies. The primary stakeholders are the data consumer and the data provider; others are parties they delegated trust to, and the owners of callout servers. Trust is delegated stepwise from either the consumer or the provider, and the entities so reached form a trust domain. A processor can belong to several, and MUST be able to report its memberships for tracing, including who delegated each privilege.

Standard protocols are used to authenticate callout servers, and strong authentication, message authentication codes and encryption SHOULD be used, though protection is optional inside a single administrative domain with strong guarantees. A separate security association MUST be used for each channel between a processor and a callout server, and channels MUST be separate for different primary parties. In-band service requests, such as an HTTP Bypass-OPES header, MUST be authenticated.

On privacy, processors MUST advise primary parties of their privacy policy and respect theirs, conveyed per flow. Digital signatures can mark changes so a third party can verify them against the originating party's policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must know who they trust to touch the parcel, helpers must show proof of who they are, and private things stay private.

sections.title: Consent, Addressability and the IAB Considerations
sections.content:
To allow verifiable integrity and end-to-end encryption, OPES processors MUST be explicitly addressable at the IP layer by the end user (a chain is fine if the first processor is addressed) and MUST be consented to by the data consumer or the data provider.

Section 4 maps the architecture to the IAB considerations: one-party consent, IP-layer communications, notification through tracing, non-blocking via HTTP extensions that let the consumer ask for a non-OPES version, URI resolution, reference validity, application addressing extensions (none required) and privacy.

The summary says the architecture has few interoperability requirements. The necessary elements are the OPES ruleset schema and the OCP requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: You must be able to find the helper yourself, and you or the shop must agree to let it help.
